This is the only film version of Hamlet I have seen fully, but I played Horatio in a stage production several years ago, and therefore have a well-rounded knowledge of the play. I would give this film a 8 out of 10 for acting, but 9.5 out of 10 for visual design, costuming, etc. Branagh is a very good Hamlet, Derek Jacobi is probably the best as Claudius, and most of the other cast is passable. The celebrity cameos were fun (Robin Williams is perfect) and harmless (except for Jack Lemmon!) The entire setting has been overhauled to the mid-19th century, which works perfectly fine, except for a few script incongruities (e.g., references to obsolete weapons and Hamlet being attacked by pirates on his way to England). Those who would condemn this change in period may forget that Shakespeare thought nothing of including cannon and other fixtures of his time when writing within ancient and medieval settings. A fresh interpretation of many scenes has been attempted, usually involving mirrors, hidden passages, and people walking through several rooms while they speak--a nice metaphorical addition to the ever-present themes of madness vs. sanity and secrecy vs. innocent ignorance. The climactic "mortality scene," which I like to call it, is excellent--not truly over the top. The actor playing Horatio was solid, and really shined when on the verge of suicide ("I am more an antique Roman than a Dane"). However, the scene that actually made the biggest impression on me was Reynaldo's (Gerard Depardieu) brief interview with Polonius. I won't spoil it other than to say it completely altered my perception of Polonius and added a whole layer of seediness to Laertes' travels in France (and by the way, it appears that he brings Paris Communards or some such folk along with him when returning to Denmark!)

The cinematography of much of the film was just awful. I agree with those who likened it to something shot with an iPhone. I suspect that this was done to imbue a sense of reality to the film's fictional portrayal of Neil Armstrong's personal life. The producers and director chose to focus more on the man and less on the crowning achievement of the American moon landing. Yes, I saw the movie despite its elimination of the symbolic capstone of the US space program - the planting the American Flag on the moon. I should have understood this willful editorial decision for the augury that it was. One would think they would try to represent the man accurately by staying true to Jim Hanson's research that underlied his book First Man. In my opinion and apparently that of many others who knew Armstrong well, this movie is a work of dishonest fiction. I'd provide links but it would violate Amazon's policy. I totally get that adapting a book to the screen is a monumental task. It necessarily requires the producers, writers and directors to distill the book's content to fit in an affordable feature length film. Sometimes they need to take liberties like rethreading its chronology for the sake of continuity and audience engagement. A gold standard for doing this well can be found in the Hanks-Spielberg screenplay adaptation of Stephen Ambrose's book "Band of Brothers". Neither the book or their HBO series papered over their subject's flaws or bad decisions. However it did not seek to delegitimize their sacrifices or the significance of their accomplishments either. Most of all, the HBO series honored and respected their service to our country. Contrast this with the First Man adaptation that seems to me to be agenda-driven - designed to take Armstrong down a notch by obsessing on his few flaws and playing down his spectacular achievements. They also diss US space program and our flag. I guess I went expecting too much from a French director (Damien Chazelle) and a Canadian actor (Ryan Gosling). If there's any fondness for Armstrong as a great American hero in this movie, I can't find it.
